Maharashtra State Board · HSC · Mathematics & Statistics (40) · Part II · Chapter 2

Applications of Derivatives

File 1 of 3 · Detailed Teaching Notes

Covers the complete textbook chapter (pp. 65–94): tangents & normals, derivative as a rate measure, velocity–acceleration–jerk, approximations, Rolle’s theorem, LMVT, increasing & decreasing functions, maxima & minima and optimisation problems. Every board question on this chapter from the six papers in your project (Mar 2024 – Jun 2026) is tagged and solved where it appears. Read this first; then use File 2 for revision and File 3 for timed practice.
Contents

How to use this chapter (read this first)

What the chapter is really about

Chapter 1 taught you how to differentiate. Chapter 2 asks: what can a derivative tell you? It turns out one number, f′(a)f'(a)f′(a), carries three different meanings, and the whole chapter is just these three meanings applied:

Meaning of f′(a)f'(a)f′(a) Topic in this chapter Typical question
Slope of the tangent at x=ax=ax=a Tangents & normals; Rolle; LMVT “Find the equation of the tangent at …”
Rate of change of yyy w.r.t. xxx Rate measure; velocity, acceleration “How fast is the area increasing …”
Local behaviour (going up / down / flat) Approximation; increasing–decreasing; maxima–minima “Find the dimensions for maximum volume”

If you remember that f′(a)f'(a)f′(a) is simultaneously a slope, a rate and a direction signal, nothing in this chapter is new — it is the same tool pointed at different problems.

The single most useful observation

In all six papers, every Chapter 2 question was either a textbook solved example or a textbook exercise question, often word-for-word with changed numbers. The chapter is short (30 pages). Solving every example and exercise in pp. 65–94 is the highest-return preparation you can do for these 9 marks.

Notice also where the marks sit: mostly 2- and 3-mark questions, with one 4-mark optimisation question in Mar 2024. Optimisation (maxima/minima word problems) is the only topic long enough to be a 4-marker.

Tangents and Normals (Textbook 2.1.2)

Intuition

Zoom in far enough on a smooth curve at a point PPP and the curve looks like a straight line. That line is the tangent at PPP. Its slope is the derivative at PPP — this is the geometrical meaning of the derivative you met in Chapter 1 (Section 1.2.1).

The normal at PPP is the line through PPP perpendicular to the tangent. Think of a ball rolling along a curved track: the tangent is the direction it moves in; the normal is the direction the track pushes on it.

The formulas and why they hold

Slopes and equations at P(x1,y1)P(x_1,y_1)P(x1​,y1​)

Slope of tangent:
m=(dydx)(x1,y1)m=\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(x_1,y_1)}m=(dxdy​)(x1​,y1​)​
Slope of normal (when m≠0m\neq0m=0):
m′=−1m=−1(dydx)(x1,y1)m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(x_1,y_1)}}m′=−m1​=−(dxdy​)(x1​,y1​)​1​
Equation of tangent: y−y1=m(x−x1)\quad y-y_1=m(x-x_1)y−y1​=m(x−x1​)

Equation of normal: y−y1=m′(x−x1)\quad y-y_1=m'(x-x_1)y−y1​=m′(x−x1​)

Why m′=−1/mm'=-1/mm′=−1/m? Two non-vertical lines with slopes m1m_1m1​, m2m_2m2​ are perpendicular exactly when m1m2=−1m_1m_2=-1m1​m2​=−1. The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so m⋅m′=−1m\cdot m'=-1m⋅m′=−1, giving m′=−1/mm'=-1/mm′=−1/m.

Why the point–slope form? A line through (x1,y1)(x_1,y_1)(x1​,y1​) with slope mmm: for any other point (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) on it, y−y1x−x1=m\dfrac{y-y_1}{x-x_1}=mx−x1​y−y1​​=m. Cross-multiplying gives y−y1=m(x−x1)y-y_1=m(x-x_1)y−y1​=m(x−x1​).

Special cases the formula hides

Situation at PPP Tangent Normal
dydx=0\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0dxdy​=0 horizontal: y=y1y=y_1y=y1​ vertical: x=x1x=x_1x=x1​
dydx\dfrac{dy}{dx}dxdy​ undefined (denominator 000, e.g. dxdy=0\dfrac{dx}{dy}=0dydx​=0) vertical: x=x1x=x_1x=x1​ horizontal: y=y1y=y_1y=y1​
Tangent parallel to a line of slope kkk set dydx=k\dfrac{dy}{dx}=kdxdy​=k —
Tangent perpendicular to a line of slope kkk set dydx=−1k\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac1kdxdy​=−k1​ —

Tangent parallel to Y-axis dxdy=0\dfrac{dx}{dy}=0dydx​=0

Slope of the line ax+by+c=0ax+by+c=0ax+by+c=0 is −ab-\dfrac{a}{b}−ba​. You will need this in almost every “parallel / perpendicular to a given line” question.

Mistakes that cost marks here
  1. Substituting the point too early. Differentiate first, then substitute (x1,y1)(x_1,y_1)(x1​,y1​). If you substitute first you are differentiating a constant and get 000.
  2. Forgetting to find the point in parametric questions. Given θ\thetaθ, you must compute both xxx and yyy before writing the equation.
  3. Sign slip in the normal. Normal slope is −1/m-1/m−1/m, not 1/m1/m1/m and not −m-m−m.
  4. Leaving the answer as y−2=12(x−12)y-2=\tfrac12(x-\tfrac12)y−2=21​(x−21​). Board answers are expected in the form ax+by+c=0ax+by+c=0ax+by+c=0 with integer coefficients. Clear fractions.

Worked examples (textbook Ex. 1 and Ex. 2, p. 66–68)

Example 1 — explicit curve [PYQ Feb 2025, Q23, 3 marks]

Find the equations of the tangent and normal to y=2x3−x2+2y=2x^3-x^2+2y=2x3−x2+2 at (12,2)\left(\tfrac12,2\right)(21​,2).

Step 1 — differentiate.
dydx=6x2−2x\frac{dy}{dx}=6x^2-2xdxdy​=6x2−2x

Step 2 — slope at the point.
m=(dydx)(12,2)=6(12)2−2(12)=32−1=12m=\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{\left(\frac12,2\right)}=6\left(\tfrac12\right)^2-2\left(\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac32-1=\tfrac12m=(dxdy​)(21​,2)​=6(21​)2−2(21​)=23​−1=21​
So the slope of the normal is m′=−1m=−2m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-2m′=−m1​=−2.

Step 3 — tangent.
y−2=12(x−12) ⇒ 4y−8=2x−1 ⇒ 2x−4y+7=0y-2=\tfrac12\left(x-\tfrac12\right)\ \Rightarrow\ 4y-8=2x-1\ \Rightarrow\ 2x-4y+7=0y−2=21​(x−21​) ⇒ 4y−8=2x−1 ⇒ 2x−4y+7=0

Step 4 — normal.
y−2=−2(x−12) ⇒ y−2=−2x+1 ⇒ 2x+y−3=0y-2=-2\left(x-\tfrac12\right)\ \Rightarrow\ y-2=-2x+1\ \Rightarrow\ 2x+y-3=0y−2=−2(x−21​) ⇒ y−2=−2x+1 ⇒ 2x+y−3=0

Check the point first: 2(18)−14+2=14−14+2=22\left(\tfrac18\right)-\tfrac14+2=\tfrac14-\tfrac14+2=22(81​)−41​+2=41​−41​+2=2. ✓ The point lies on the curve. Doing this check takes five seconds and catches copying errors in the question.

Example 2 — implicit curve

Find the tangent and normal to x3+2x2y−9xy=−2x^3+2x^2y-9xy=-2x3+2x2y−9xy=−2 at (2,1)(2,1)(2,1).

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. xxx. The term 2x2y2x^2y2x2y is a product, so use the product rule:
3x2+2[x2dydx+2xy]−9[xdydx+y]=03x^2+2\left[x^2\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy\right]-9\left[x\frac{dy}{dx}+y\right]=03x2+2[x2dxdy​+2xy]−9[xdxdy​+y]=0
3x2+2x2dydx+4xy−9xdydx−9y=03x^2+2x^2\frac{dy}{dx}+4xy-9x\frac{dy}{dx}-9y=03x2+2x2dxdy​+4xy−9xdxdy​−9y=0
Collect the dydx\dfrac{dy}{dx}dxdy​ terms:
(2x2−9x)dydx=9y−4xy−3x2⇒dydx=9y−4xy−3x22x2−9x(2x^2-9x)\frac{dy}{dx}=9y-4xy-3x^2\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{9y-4xy-3x^2}{2x^2-9x}(2x2−9x)dxdy​=9y−4xy−3x2⇒dxdy​=2x2−9x9y−4xy−3x2​
At (2,1)(2,1)(2,1):
m=9−8−128−18=−11−10=1110m=\frac{9-8-12}{8-18}=\frac{-11}{-10}=\frac{11}{10}m=8−189−8−12​=−10−11​=1011​

A known error in the textbook

The textbook solution of this example (p. 66) writes the denominator as 2(4)−9(1)=−12(4)-9(1)=-12(4)−9(1)=−1 and gets m=11m=11m=11. That is an arithmetic slip: the denominator is 2x2−9x2x^2-9x2x2−9x evaluated at x=2x=2x=2, which is 8−18=−108-18=-108−18=−10. The correct slope is 1110\tfrac{11}{10}1011​, giving

Tangent: y−1=1110(x−2) ⇒ 11x−10y−12=0y-1=\tfrac{11}{10}(x-2)\ \Rightarrow\ 11x-10y-12=0y−1=1011​(x−2) ⇒ 11x−10y−12=0

Normal: y−1=−1011(x−2) ⇒ 10x+11y−31=0y-1=-\tfrac{10}{11}(x-2)\ \Rightarrow\ 10x+11y-31=0y−1=−1110​(x−2) ⇒ 10x+11y−31=0

If this exact question appears, write the correct working. Examiners mark the mathematics, not the textbook’s typo.

Example 3 — parametric curve

Find the tangent and normal to x=2sin⁡3θx=2\sin^3\thetax=2sin3θ, y=3cos⁡3θy=3\cos^3\thetay=3cos3θ at θ=π4\theta=\dfrac\pi4θ=4π​.

dxdθ=6sin⁡2θcos⁡θ,dydθ=−9cos⁡2θsin⁡θ\frac{dx}{d\theta}=6\sin^2\theta\cos\theta,\qquad\frac{dy}{d\theta}=-9\cos^2\theta\sin\thetadθdx​=6sin2θcosθ,dθdy​=−9cos2θsinθ
dydx=−9cos⁡2θsin⁡θ6sin⁡2θcos⁡θ=−32cot⁡θ⇒m=−32cot⁡π4=−32,m′=23\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-9\cos^2\theta\sin\theta}{6\sin^2\theta\cos\theta}=-\frac32\cot\theta\quad\Rightarrow\quad m=-\frac32\cot\frac\pi4=-\frac32,\qquad m'=\frac23dxdy​=6sin2θcosθ−9cos2θsinθ​=−23​cotθ⇒m=−23​cot4π​=−23​,m′=32​

The point (do not skip): x=2(12)3=12x=2\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^3=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}x=2(2​1​)3=2​1​,  y=3(12)3=322\ y=3\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^3=\tfrac{3}{2\sqrt2} y=3(2​1​)3=22​3​.

Tangent:
y−322=−32(x−12) ⇒ 3x+2y−32=0y-\frac{3}{2\sqrt2}=-\frac32\left(x-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\ \Rightarrow\ 3x+2y-3\sqrt2=0y−22​3​=−23​(x−2​1​) ⇒ 3x+2y−32​=0
Normal (multiply through by 626\sqrt262​ to clear fractions):
y−322=23(x−12) ⇒ 42 x−62 y+5=0y-\frac{3}{2\sqrt2}=\frac23\left(x-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\ \Rightarrow\ 4\sqrt2\,x-6\sqrt2\,y+5=0y−22​3​=32​(x−2​1​) ⇒ 42​x−62​y+5=0

Check of the normal’s constant: 62⋅322=96\sqrt2\cdot\tfrac{3}{2\sqrt2}=962​⋅22​3​=9 and 62⋅23⋅12=46\sqrt2\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac1{\sqrt2}=462​⋅32​⋅2​1​=4, so 62 y−9=42 x−46\sqrt2\,y-9=4\sqrt2\,x-462​y−9=42​x−4, i.e. 42x−62y+5=04\sqrt2x-6\sqrt2y+5=042​x−62​y+5=0. ✓

Example 4 — tangent parallel to a line [PYQ Jul 2024 Q9; Jul 2025 Q10, 2 marks]

Find the points on y=x3−6x2+x+3y=x^3-6x^2+x+3y=x3−6x2+x+3 where the tangents are parallel to y=x+5y=x+5y=x+5.

The line y=x+5y=x+5y=x+5 has slope 111. Parallel lines have equal slopes, so set dydx=1\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1dxdy​=1:
3x2−12x+1=1 ⇒ 3x(x−4)=0 ⇒ x=0 or x=43x^2-12x+1=1\ \Rightarrow\ 3x(x-4)=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=0\ \text{or}\ x=43x2−12x+1=1 ⇒ 3x(x−4)=0 ⇒ x=0 or x=4
x=0x=0x=0: y=3y=3y=3. x=4\quad x=4x=4: y=64−96+4+3=−25y=64-96+4+3=-25y=64−96+4+3=−25.

Required points: (0,3)(0,3)(0,3) and (4,−25)(4,-25)(4,−25).

The Jul 2025 version asked you to show that the tangent at (0,3)(0,3)(0,3) is parallel to y=x+5y=x+5y=x+5. Same work, reversed: compute (dydx)(0,3)=3(0)−0+1=1\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(0,3)}=3(0)-0+1=1(dxdy​)(0,3)​=3(0)−0+1=1, which equals the slope of the line, hence parallel.

More exercise patterns (Ex. 2.1, Q1–Q6, Misc. 2)

Tangent perpendicular to a line (Ex. 2.1 Q2)

Find the point on y=x−3y=\sqrt{x-3}y=x−3​ where the tangent is perpendicular to 6x+3y−5=06x+3y-5=06x+3y−5=0.

Slope of the line =−63=−2=-\tfrac63=-2=−36​=−2. Perpendicular slope =12=\tfrac12=21​.
dydx=12x−3=12 ⇒ x−3=1 ⇒ x=4, y=1\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-3}}=\frac12\ \Rightarrow\ \sqrt{x-3}=1\ \Rightarrow\ x=4,\ y=1dxdy​=2x−3​1​=21​ ⇒ x−3​=1 ⇒ x=4, y=1
Point: (4,1)(4,1)(4,1).

Tangents parallel to the X-axis (Ex. 2.1 Q4)

Find the tangents to x2+y2−2x−4y+1=0x^2+y^2-2x-4y+1=0x2+y2−2x−4y+1=0 that are parallel to the X-axis.

2x+2ydydx−2−4dydx=0 ⇒ dydx=1−xy−22x+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}-2-4\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1-x}{y-2}2x+2ydxdy​−2−4dxdy​=0 ⇒ dxdy​=y−21−x​.

Parallel to X-axis ⇒dydx=0⇒x=1\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0\Rightarrow x=1⇒dxdy​=0⇒x=1. Substitute in the curve: 1+y2−2−4y+1=0⇒y(y−4)=0⇒y=01+y^2-2-4y+1=0\Rightarrow y(y-4)=0\Rightarrow y=01+y2−2−4y+1=0⇒y(y−4)=0⇒y=0 or 444.

Points (1,0)(1,0)(1,0), (1,4)(1,4)(1,4); tangents y=0y=0y=0 and y=4y=4y=4.

The curve is a circle with centre (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) and radius 222, so the horizontal tangents touch it at the bottom (y=0y=0y=0) and top (y=4y=4y=4). Geometry confirms the calculus.

Normals parallel to a line (Ex. 2.1 Q5)

Find the equations of the normals to 3x2−y2=83x^2-y^2=83x2−y2=8 parallel to x+3y=4x+3y=4x+3y=4.

6x−2ydydx=0⇒dydx=3xy6x-2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3x}{y}6x−2ydxdy​=0⇒dxdy​=y3x​, so slope of normal =−y3x=-\dfrac{y}{3x}=−3xy​.

Slope of x+3y=4x+3y=4x+3y=4 is −13-\tfrac13−31​. Set −y3x=−13⇒y=x-\dfrac{y}{3x}=-\dfrac13\Rightarrow y=x−3xy​=−31​⇒y=x.

Substitute: 3x2−x2=8⇒x2=4⇒x=±23x^2-x^2=8\Rightarrow x^2=4\Rightarrow x=\pm23x2−x2=8⇒x2=4⇒x=±2. Points (2,2)(2,2)(2,2) and (−2,−2)(-2,-2)(−2,−2).

Normal at (2,2)(2,2)(2,2): y−2=−13(x−2)⇒x+3y−8=0y-2=-\tfrac13(x-2)\Rightarrow x+3y-8=0y−2=−31​(x−2)⇒x+3y−8=0.

Normal at (−2,−2)(-2,-2)(−2,−2): y+2=−13(x+2)⇒x+3y+8=0y+2=-\tfrac13(x+2)\Rightarrow x+3y+8=0y+2=−31​(x+2)⇒x+3y+8=0.

Line touching a curve: find constants (Ex. 2.1 Q6)

If y=4x−5y=4x-5y=4x−5 touches y2=ax3+by^2=ax^3+by2=ax3+b at (2,3)(2,3)(2,3), find aaa and bbb.

“Touches at (2,3)(2,3)(2,3)” gives two conditions: the point is on the curve, and the curve’s slope there equals the line’s slope 444.

Slope: 2ydydx=3ax2⇒(dydx)(2,3)=3a(4)2(3)=2a=4⇒a=22y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3ax^2\Rightarrow\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(2,3)}=\dfrac{3a(4)}{2(3)}=2a=4\Rightarrow a=22ydxdy​=3ax2⇒(dxdy​)(2,3)​=2(3)3a(4)​=2a=4⇒a=2.

Point on curve: 9=2(8)+b⇒b=−79=2(8)+b\Rightarrow b=-79=2(8)+b⇒b=−7.

Tangent and normal for an implicit quartic (Misc. II Q3)

Find the tangent and normal to y4−4x4−6xy=0y^4-4x^4-6xy=0y4−4x4−6xy=0 at M(1,2)M(1,2)M(1,2).

4y3dydx−16x3−6(xdydx+y)=0⇒dydx=16x3+6y4y3−6x4y^3\dfrac{dy}{dx}-16x^3-6\left(x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\right)=0\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{16x^3+6y}{4y^3-6x}4y3dxdy​−16x3−6(xdxdy​+y)=0⇒dxdy​=4y3−6x16x3+6y​.

At (1,2)(1,2)(1,2): m=16+1232−6=2826=1413m=\dfrac{16+12}{32-6}=\dfrac{28}{26}=\dfrac{14}{13}m=32−616+12​=2628​=1314​.

Tangent: y−2=1413(x−1)⇒14x−13y+12=0y-2=\tfrac{14}{13}(x-1)\Rightarrow14x-13y+12=0y−2=1314​(x−1)⇒14x−13y+12=0. Normal: y−2=−1314(x−1)⇒13x+14y−41=0y-2=-\tfrac{13}{14}(x-1)\Rightarrow13x+14y-41=0y−2=−1413​(x−1)⇒13x+14y−41=0.

Triangle formed by a tangent and the axes (Misc. II Q2)

Find the area of the triangle formed by the tangent to y=3−x2y=3-x^2y=3−x2 at (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) and the coordinate axes.

dydx=−2x⇒m=−2\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2x\Rightarrow m=-2dxdy​=−2x⇒m=−2. Tangent: y−2=−2(x−1)⇒2x+y=4y-2=-2(x-1)\Rightarrow2x+y=4y−2=−2(x−1)⇒2x+y=4.

Intercepts: X-axis at (2,0)(2,0)(2,0), Y-axis at (0,4)(0,4)(0,4). Area =12×2×4=4=\tfrac12\times2\times4=4=21​×2×4=4 sq. units.

Orthogonal curves (Misc. II Q1) — a proof-type question

Claim. If ax2+by2=1ax^2+by^2=1ax2+by2=1 and a′x2+b′y2=1a'x^2+b'y^2=1a′x2+b′y2=1 cut orthogonally, then 1a−1b=1a′−1b′\dfrac1a-\dfrac1b=\dfrac1{a'}-\dfrac1{b'}a1​−b1​=a′1​−b′1​.

Proof. Let (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) be a point of intersection. Differentiating each curve:
m1=−axby,m2=−a′xb′ym_1=-\frac{ax}{by},\qquad m_2=-\frac{a'x}{b'y}m1​=−byax​,m2​=−b′ya′x​
Orthogonal means the tangents are perpendicular: m1m2=−1m_1m_2=-1m1​m2​=−1, so
aa′x2bb′y2=−1 ⇒ x2y2=−bb′aa′(i)\frac{aa'x^2}{bb'y^2}=-1\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{x^2}{y^2}=-\frac{bb'}{aa'}\qquad\text{(i)}bb′y2aa′x2​=−1 ⇒ y2x2​=−aa′bb′​(i)
Subtracting the two curve equations: (a−a′)x2+(b−b′)y2=0(a-a')x^2+(b-b')y^2=0(a−a′)x2+(b−b′)y2=0, so
x2y2=b′−ba−a′(ii)\frac{x^2}{y^2}=\frac{b'-b}{a-a'}\qquad\text{(ii)}y2x2​=a−a′b′−b​(ii)
Equating (i) and (ii): aa′(b′−b)=−bb′(a−a′)aa'(b'-b)=-bb'(a-a')aa′(b′−b)=−bb′(a−a′). Divide both sides by aa′bb′aa'bb'aa′bb′:
b′−bbb′=−a−a′aa′ ⇒ 1b−1b′=1a−1a′ ⇒ 1a−1b=1a′−1b′.■\frac{b'-b}{bb'}=-\frac{a-a'}{aa'}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac1b-\frac1{b'}=\frac1a-\frac1{a'}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac1a-\frac1b=\frac1{a'}-\frac1{b'}.\qquad\blacksquarebb′b′−b​=−aa′a−a′​ ⇒ b1​−b′1​=a1​−a′1​ ⇒ a1​−b1​=a′1​−b′1​.■

Derivative as a Rate Measure (Textbook 2.1.3)

Intuition: average vs instantaneous rate

If y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) and xxx changes from x1x_1x1​ to x2x_2x2​, the average rate of change is
δyδx=f(x2)−f(x1)x2−x1,\frac{\delta y}{\delta x}=\frac{f(x_2)-f(x_1)}{x_2-x_1},δxδy​=x2​−x1​f(x2​)−f(x1​)​,
the slope of the chord (secant) joining the two points. Let x2→x1x_2\to x_1x2​→x1​ and the chord turns into the tangent; the limit is the instantaneous rate of change f′(x1)f'(x_1)f′(x1​).

Your car’s trip computer shows average speed (total distance ÷ total time). The speedometer shows instantaneous speed — that is the derivative.

Related rates: the method

Most rate problems involve two or more quantities that all change with time ttt, linked by a geometric formula. The chain rule then links their rates.

Five-step method for every related-rates question
  1. Name every changing quantity with a letter (they are all functions of ttt). Draw a figure if there is geometry.
  2. Write what is given as a rate (drdt=5\dfrac{dr}{dt}=5dtdr​=5) and what is asked (dAdt=?\dfrac{dA}{dt}=?dtdA​=?) and the instant (“when r=8r=8r=8”).
  3. Find a formula linking the quantities (area, volume, Pythagoras, similar triangles). Use fixed constants to eliminate unwanted variables before differentiating.
  4. Differentiate w.r.t. ttt using the chain rule: ddt(r2)=2rdrdt\dfrac{d}{dt}(r^2)=2r\dfrac{dr}{dt}dtd​(r2)=2rdtdr​.
  5. Substitute the instant’s values only now, solve, and write the answer with units and the words “increasing” or “decreasing”.
The classic trap

Never substitute a value that changes (like r=8r=8r=8) before differentiating — it turns a variable into a constant and its derivative into 000. Only genuine constants (like a fixed base radius of 333 m, or a fixed tan⁡30∘\tan30^\circtan30∘) may be substituted before differentiating.

Units: if area is in cm² and time in sec, dAdt\dfrac{dA}{dt}dtdA​ is in cm²/sec. The textbook itself sometimes writes “cc/sec” for a radius rate (Ex. 2, p. 69); that is a misprint — a rate of radius is in cm/sec.

Worked examples

Circular wave [PYQ Feb 2026 Q12, 2 marks — same as textbook Ex. 1 with changed numbers]

A stone dropped into a quiet lake makes circular waves. The radius increases at 333 cm/sec. How fast is the enclosed area increasing when the radius is 888 cm?

Let RRR = radius, AAA = area at time ttt. A=πR2A=\pi R^2A=πR2.

Differentiate w.r.t. ttt: dAdt=2πRdRdt\dfrac{dA}{dt}=2\pi R\dfrac{dR}{dt}dtdA​=2πRdtdR​.

Given dRdt=3\dfrac{dR}{dt}=3dtdR​=3; when R=8R=8R=8: dAdt=2π(8)(3)=48π\dfrac{dA}{dt}=2\pi(8)(3)=48\pidtdA​=2π(8)(3)=48π.

The area is increasing at 48π48\pi48π cm²/sec.

(The textbook version uses 555 cm/sec, giving 80π80\pi80π cm²/sec.)

V=43πR3⇒dVdt=4πR2dRdtV=\tfrac43\pi R^3\Rightarrow\dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pi R^2\dfrac{dR}{dt}V=34​πR3⇒dtdV​=4πR2dtdR​. With dVdt=4π\dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pidtdV​=4π:  dRdt=1R2\ \dfrac{dR}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{R^2} dtdR​=R21​.

When V=288πV=288\piV=288π: 43πR3=288π⇒R3=216⇒R=6\tfrac43\pi R^3=288\pi\Rightarrow R^3=216\Rightarrow R=634​πR3=288π⇒R3=216⇒R=6. So dRdt=136\dfrac{dR}{dt}=\dfrac1{36}dtdR​=361​ cm/sec.

S=4πR2⇒dSdt=8πRdRdt=8π(6)(136)=4π3S=4\pi R^2\Rightarrow\dfrac{dS}{dt}=8\pi R\dfrac{dR}{dt}=8\pi(6)\left(\tfrac1{36}\right)=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}S=4πR2⇒dtdS​=8πRdtdR​=8π(6)(361​)=34π​ cm²/sec.

Water poured into a cylinder [PYQ Jul 2025 Q21, 3 marks]

Water is poured at 272727 m³/sec into a cylindrical vessel of base radius 333 m. Find the rate at which the water level rises.

Let HHH = height of water, VVV = volume. The radius is fixed at 333, so substitute it now:
V=π(3)2H=9πH ⇒ dVdt=9πdHdtV=\pi(3)^2H=9\pi H\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dV}{dt}=9\pi\frac{dH}{dt}V=π(3)2H=9πH ⇒ dtdV​=9πdtdH​
27=9πdHdt ⇒ dHdt=3π m/sec27=9\pi\frac{dH}{dt}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dH}{dt}=\frac{3}{\pi}\ \text{m/sec}27=9πdtdH​ ⇒ dtdH​=π3​ m/sec
The water level rises at 3π\dfrac3\piπ3​ m/sec (textbook Ex. 3 uses 363636 m³/sec, giving 4π\dfrac4\piπ4​ m/sec).

Lamp-post and shadow (textbook Ex. 4)

A man 180180180 cm tall walks away from a 4.54.54.5 m lamp post at 1.21.21.2 m/sec. Find the rate at which (i) his shadow lengthens, (ii) the tip of the shadow moves.

Triangles BMNBMNBMN and BOABOABOA are similar (both right-angled, common angle at BBB):
MNOA=BMBO ⇒ 1.84.5=xx+y ⇒ 1.8x+1.8y=4.5x ⇒ x=2y3\frac{MN}{OA}=\frac{BM}{BO}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{1.8}{4.5}=\frac{x}{x+y}\ \Rightarrow\ 1.8x+1.8y=4.5x\ \Rightarrow\ x=\frac{2y}{3}OAMN​=BOBM​ ⇒ 4.51.8​=x+yx​ ⇒ 1.8x+1.8y=4.5x ⇒ x=32y​
Differentiate: dxdt=23dydt=23(1.2)=0.8\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac23\dfrac{dy}{dt}=\dfrac23(1.2)=0.8dtdx​=32​dtdy​=32​(1.2)=0.8 m/sec.

Tip of the shadow is at distance x+yx+yx+y from the post: ddt(x+y)=0.8+1.2=2\dfrac{d}{dt}(x+y)=0.8+1.2=2dtd​(x+y)=0.8+1.2=2 m/sec.

Shadow lengthens at 0.80.80.8 m/sec; its tip moves at 222 m/sec.

Notice the shortcut: the rate is constant — it does not depend on where the man is. That is why no “when he is … m away” is given.

Man 1.51.51.5 m, lamp 4.54.54.5 m, walking towards it at 34\tfrac3443​ m/sec.

1.54.5=xx+y⇒3x=x+y⇒x=y2\dfrac{1.5}{4.5}=\dfrac{x}{x+y}\Rightarrow3x=x+y\Rightarrow x=\dfrac y24.51.5​=x+yx​⇒3x=x+y⇒x=2y​. Walking towards the post means yyy decreases: dydt=−34\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\dfrac34dtdy​=−43​.

Sliding ladder (Ex. 2.1 Q15)

A 101010 m ladder leans on a wall. The bottom is pulled away at 1.21.21.2 m/sec. How fast does the top slide down when the bottom is 666 m from the wall?

Let xxx = distance of foot from wall, yyy = height of top. Pythagoras: x2+y2=100x^2+y^2=100x2+y2=100.

Differentiate: 2xdxdt+2ydydt=0⇒dydt=−xydxdt2x\dfrac{dx}{dt}+2y\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\dfrac xy\dfrac{dx}{dt}2xdtdx​+2ydtdy​=0⇒dtdy​=−yx​dtdx​.

When x=6x=6x=6: y=100−36=8y=\sqrt{100-36}=8y=100−36​=8.  dydt=−68(1.2)=−0.9\ \dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\dfrac68(1.2)=-0.9 dtdy​=−86​(1.2)=−0.9.

The top slides down at 0.90.90.9 m/sec. (Negative sign = height decreasing.)

v=dsdt,a=dvdt=d2sdt2,j=dadt=d3sdt3v=\frac{ds}{dt},\qquad a=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{d^2s}{dt^2},\qquad j=\frac{da}{dt}=\frac{d^3s}{dt^3}v=dtds​,a=dtdv​=dt2d2s​,j=dtda​=dt3d3s​

s(t)=2t2+3t−4s(t)=2t^2+3t-4s(t)=2t2+3t−4, 0≤t≤40\le t\le40≤t≤4. Average velocity =s(4)−s(0)4−0=40−(−4)4=11=\dfrac{s(4)-s(0)}{4-0}=\dfrac{40-(-4)}{4}=11=4−0s(4)−s(0)​=440−(−4)​=11. Instantaneous v=4t+3=11⇒t=2v=4t+3=11\Rightarrow t=2v=4t+3=11⇒t=2. So c=2c=2c=2.

This is LMVT in disguise: some instant has velocity equal to the average velocity.

Approximations (Textbook 2.2.1)

Intuition

Near the point x=ax=ax=a, a smooth curve is almost indistinguishable from its tangent line. So to estimate fff at a nearby point a+ha+ha+h, walk along the tangent instead of the curve: start at height f(a)f(a)f(a) and rise by (slope ×\times× run) =f′(a)⋅h=f'(a)\cdot h=f′(a)⋅h.

Derivation

By definition, f′(a)=lim⁡h→0f(a+h)−f(a)hf'(a)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}f′(a)=h→0lim​hf(a+h)−f(a)​. For a sufficiently small hhh the quotient is close to its limit:
f′(a)≈f(a+h)−f(a)h ⇒ hf′(a)≈f(a+h)−f(a)f'(a)\approx\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\ \Rightarrow\ hf'(a)\approx f(a+h)-f(a)f′(a)≈hf(a+h)−f(a)​ ⇒ hf′(a)≈f(a+h)−f(a)

Approximation formula

f(a+h)≈f(a)+h f′(a)f(a+h)\approx f(a)+h\,f'(a)f(a+h)≈f(a)+hf′(a)
Choose aaa so that f(a)f(a)f(a) and f′(a)f'(a)f′(a) are easy to compute exactly, and h=(given value)−ah=(\text{given value})-ah=(given value)−a is small. hhh may be negative.

Two errors examiners see every year
  1. Degrees in trigonometry. hhh must be in radians. Use the given 1∘=0.0175c1^\circ=0.0175^c1∘=0.0175c; so 30′=12∘=0.00875c30'=\tfrac12^\circ=0.00875^c30′=21​∘=0.00875c and 40′=23∘=0.011667c40'=\tfrac23^\circ=0.011667^c40′=32​∘=0.011667c. Using h=0.5h=0.5h=0.5 is wrong by a factor of 575757.

Rolle’s Theorem and Lagrange’s Mean Value Theorem (Textbook 2.3)

Rolle’s Theorem

Rolle’s Theorem

If a real-valued function fff is

  1. continuous on the closed interval [a,b][a,b][a,b],
  2. differentiable on the open interval (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), and
  3. f(a)=f(b)f(a)=f(b)f(a)=f(b),

then there exists at least one c∈(a,b)c\in(a,b)c∈(a,b) such that f′(c)=0f'(c)=0f′(c)=0.

Intuition. You drive from home and come back home. Your position started and ended at the same value. Somewhere in between you must have turned around — at that instant your velocity was zero. Rolle’s theorem is that statement for graphs.

Geometrical meaning. If the graph is unbroken (continuity), smooth with a tangent everywhere inside (differentiability), and the end-points are at the same height, then somewhere between them the tangent is parallel to the X-axis.

Why each condition matters

A theorem’s conditions are not decoration. Remove any one and the conclusion can fail:

Condition dropped Counter-example What goes wrong
Continuity on [a,b][a,b][a,b] f(x)=xf(x)=xf(x)=x on [0,1)[0,1)[0,1), f(1)=0f(1)=0f(1)=0 jump at x=1x=1x=1; f′(x)=1≠0f'(x)=1\neq0f′(x)=1=0 everywhere
Differentiability on (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) f(x)=∣x∣f(x)=\lvert x\rvertf(x)=∣x∣ on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] sharp corner at 000; f′=±1f'=\pm1f′=±1, never 000
f(a)=f(b)f(a)=f(b)f(a)=f(b) f(x)=xf(x)=xf(x)=x on [0,1][0,1][0,1] always rising; f′=1f'=1f′=1

Also: the theorem guarantees at least one ccc. There may be more (see Example below with two values of ccc).

Which functions are continuous and differentiable?

You must state these conditions in answers. Standard facts you may quote:

  • Polynomials are continuous and differentiable everywhere.
  • sin⁡x\sin xsinx, cos⁡x\cos xcosx, exe^xex are continuous and differentiable everywhere; log⁡x\log xlogx for x>0x>0x>0; a quotient wherever its denominator ≠0\neq0=0; g(x)\sqrt{g(x)}g(x)​ is differentiable where g(x)>0g(x)>0g(x)>0.
  • Sums, products and compositions of such functions inherit these properties on the common domain.
  • Danger signs: ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣, fractional powers like x2/3x^{2/3}x2/3 (derivative blows up at 000), piecewise definitions (check the joining point), denominators vanishing inside [a,b][a,b][a,b].

Method for “verify Rolle’s theorem”

Answer template (3 marks)
  1. State: fff is continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b] and differentiable on (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) — with the reason (polynomial / composition of continuous functions …).
  2. Compute f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b)f(b)f(b); show they are equal.
  3. Conclude: “all conditions of Rolle’s theorem are satisfied”.
  4. Find f′(x)f'(x)f′(x), solve f′(c)=0f'(c)=0f′(c)=0.
  5. Show c∈(a,b)c\in(a,b)c∈(a,b). Write “Hence Rolle’s theorem is verified.”

f(x)f(x)f(x) is a polynomial, hence continuous on [1,4][1,4][1,4] and differentiable on (1,4)(1,4)(1,4).

f(1)=1−5+9=5f(1)=1-5+9=5f(1)=1−5+9=5;  f(4)=16−20+9=5\ f(4)=16-20+9=5 f(4)=16−20+9=5. So f(1)=f(4)f(1)=f(4)f(1)=f(4).

All conditions of Rolle’s theorem are satisfied. f′(x)=2x−5f'(x)=2x-5f′(x)=2x−5.

f′(c)=0⇒2c−5=0⇒c=52=2.5∈(1,4)f'(c)=0\Rightarrow2c-5=0\Rightarrow c=\dfrac52=2.5\in(1,4)f′(c)=0⇒2c−5=0⇒c=25​=2.5∈(1,4). Hence Rolle’s theorem is verified.

Lagrange’s Mean Value Theorem (LMVT)

Lagrange’s Mean Value Theorem

If fff is continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b] and differentiable on (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), then there exists at least one c∈(a,b)c\in(a,b)c∈(a,b) such that
f′(c)=f(b)−f(a)b−a.f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.f′(c)=b−af(b)−f(a)​.

Intuition. You drive 120120120 km in 222 hours: average speed 606060 km/h. LMVT says that at some instant the speedometer read exactly 606060. (This is how average-speed toll cameras justify a fine.)

Geometrical meaning. The right side is the slope of the chord ABABAB joining (a,f(a))(a,f(a))(a,f(a)) and (b,f(b))(b,f(b))(b,f(b)). So somewhere between, the tangent is parallel to the chord.

Relation to Rolle. If f(a)=f(b)f(a)=f(b)f(a)=f(b), the chord is horizontal and LMVT becomes Rolle’s theorem. Rolle is the special case; LMVT is the tilted version.

Rolle / LMVT mistakes
  • Not stating continuity and differentiability with a reason. That is a method mark.
  • Finding ccc but not checking c∈(a,b)c\in(a,b)c∈(a,b) — or keeping a root outside the interval.
  • Using a closed interval for differentiability. It is open (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) for differentiability, closed [a,b][a,b][a,b] for continuity.
  • Saying “Rolle’s theorem is false” when a condition fails. Correct phrasing: “Rolle’s theorem is not applicable.”

Increasing and Decreasing Functions (Textbook 2.4.1)

Definitions

Strictly increasing / decreasing on an interval

fff is strictly increasing on an interval III if for all x1,x2∈Ix_1,x_2\in Ix1​,x2​∈I: x1<x2⇒f(x1)<f(x2)x_1<x_2\Rightarrow f(x_1)<f(x_2)x1​<x2​⇒f(x1​)<f(x2​).

fff is strictly decreasing on III if x1<x2⇒f(x1)>f(x2)x_1<x_2\Rightarrow f(x_1)>f(x_2)x1​<x2​⇒f(x1​)>f(x2​).

Going left to right, an increasing graph climbs; a decreasing graph falls.

Link with the derivative

The textbook shows (p. 80–81): if fff is increasing, every difference quotient f(x+h)−f(x)h>0\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}>0hf(x+h)−f(x)​>0, so its limit f′(x)≥0f'(x)\ge0f′(x)≥0. Conversely, if f′(a)>0f'(a)>0f′(a)>0, then in a small neighbourhood f(a−h)<f(a)<f(a+h)f(a-h)<f(a)<f(a+h)f(a−h)<f(a)<f(a+h).

Derivative test (as stated in the textbook’s ‘Let us Remember’)
Condition Conclusion
f′(x)>0f'(x)>0f′(x)>0 on an interval fff is strictly (monotonically) increasing there
f′(x)<0f'(x)<0f′(x)<0 on an interval fff is strictly decreasing there
f′(x)≥0f'(x)\ge0f′(x)≥0 fff is increasing
f′(x)≤0f'(x)\le0f′(x)≤0 fff is decreasing
A subtle point that the strong student should know

f′(x)>0f'(x)>0f′(x)>0 is sufficient, not necessary, for strictly increasing. f(x)=x3f(x)=x^3f(x)=x3 is strictly increasing on R\mathbb RR although f′(0)=0f'(0)=0f′(0)=0. Isolated points where f′=0f'=0f′=0 do not stop a function from being strictly increasing. This is why the textbook accepts f′(x)=3(x+2)2≥0f'(x)=3(x+2)^2\ge0f′(x)=3(x+2)2≥0 as showing x3+6x2+12x−5x^3+6x^2+12x-5x3+6x2+12x−5 is increasing (Ex. 2).

VSA [PYQ Feb 2025 Q2(iv), 1 mark]: Condition for f(x)f(x)f(x) to be strictly increasing for all x∈Rx\in\mathbb Rx∈R:  f′(x)>0\ f'(x)>0 f′(x)>0 for all x∈Rx\in\mathbb Rx∈R.

Method: finding intervals of increase/decrease

  1. Find f′(x)f'(x)f′(x) and factorise it fully.
  2. Solve f′(x)=0f'(x)=0f′(x)=0 (and note points where f′f'f′ is undefined or fff is undefined). These split the real line.
  3. Test the sign of f′f'f′ in each piece (pick a test value, or use the sign of each factor).
  4. f′>0f'>0f′>0 pieces: increasing. f′<0f'<0f′<0 pieces: decreasing.

Maxima and Minima (Textbook 2.4.2 – 2.4.4)

Definitions

Local maximum and local minimum

fff has a local maximum at x=cx=cx=c if f(c)>f(x)f(c)>f(x)f(c)>f(x) for all x≠cx\neq cx=c in some small interval (c−δ,c+δ)(c-\delta,c+\delta)(c−δ,c+δ). Then f(c)f(c)f(c) is a local maximum value.

fff has a local minimum at x=cx=cx=c if f(c)<f(x)f(c)<f(x)f(c)<f(x) for all x≠cx\neq cx=c near ccc.

“Local” matters: a local maximum is the top of a hill, not necessarily the highest point of the whole mountain range. A local maximum value can even be smaller than a local minimum value elsewhere.

A point where f′(c)=0f'(c)=0f′(c)=0 is called a stationary (turning) point: the tangent is horizontal. Extreme values occur at such points (for differentiable fff), but not every stationary point is an extreme — see points of inflexion.

First derivative test

First derivative test (hhh a small positive number)
f′(c)f'(c)f′(c) sign of f′f'f′ just left (c−hc-hc−h) sign just right (c+hc+hc+h) Conclusion
000 +++ (rising) −-− (falling) local maximum
000 −-− (falling) +++ (rising) local minimum
000 same sign on both sides neither — point of inflexion (e.g. x3x^3x3 at 000)

Second derivative test

Second derivative test

If f′(c)=0f'(c)=0f′(c)=0 and

  • f′′(c)<0f''(c)<0f′′(c)<0: local maximum at ccc (slope is decreasing through zero: +→0→−+\to0\to-+→0→−).
  • f′′(c)>0f''(c)>0f′′(c)>0: local minimum at ccc (slope increasing: −→0→+-\to0\to+−→0→+).
  • f′′(c)=0f''(c)=0f′′(c)=0: the test fails; use the first derivative test.

Memory trick: a smiling face ⌣\smile⌣ has positive curvature and sits at a minimum; a frowning face ⌢\frown⌢ (f′′<0f''<0f′′<0) is at a maximum. “f′′f''f′′ positive — cup holds water — minimum.”

Maximum 54\dfrac5445​ when sin⁡x=12\sin x=\dfrac12sinx=21​; minimum when (s−12)2\left(s-\tfrac12\right)^2(s−21​)2 is largest, i.e. s=−1s=-1s=−1: f=1−1−1=−1f=1-1-1=-1f=1−1−1=−1.

(By derivatives: f′(x)=cos⁡x(1−2sin⁡x)=0f'(x)=\cos x(1-2\sin x)=0f′(x)=cosx(1−2sinx)=0 gives the same stationary points.)

Other Ex. 2.4 Q9 answers: (i) y=5x3+2x2−3xy=5x^3+2x^2-3xy=5x3+2x2−3x: max at x=−35x=-\tfrac35x=−53​ (value 3625\tfrac{36}{25}2536​), min at x=13x=\tfrac13x=31​ (value −1627-\tfrac{16}{27}−2716​); (iii) x3−9x2+24xx^3-9x^2+24xx3−9x2+24x: max 202020 at x=2x=2x=2, min 161616 at x=4x=4x=4; (iv) x2+16x2x^2+\dfrac{16}{x^2}x2+x216​: min 888 at x=±2x=\pm2x=±2.

Optimisation Problems (word problems on maxima and minima)

This is the only part of the chapter that regularly becomes a 4-mark question. The mathematics is easy; the setting-up is where students lose marks.

Six-step method
  1. Draw and name. Assign letters to all lengths. Decide what is to be maximised/minimised (the objective).
  2. Constraint. Write the fixed condition (perimeter, area, volume, sum …) as an equation.
  3. One variable. Use the constraint to write the objective in terms of a single variable.
  4. Differentiate and equate to zero. Solve; reject values that are meaningless (negative lengths, zero dimensions).
  5. Second derivative test to confirm maximum or minimum.
  6. Answer the question asked — dimensions, or the maximum value, with units.
Divide 20 into two parts with minimum sum of squares [PYQ Feb 2025 Q9, 2 marks]

Let the parts be xxx and 20−x20-x20−x. S=x2+(20−x)2S=x^2+(20-x)^2S=x2+(20−x)2.

dSdx=2x−2(20−x)=4x−40=0⇒x=10\dfrac{dS}{dx}=2x-2(20-x)=4x-40=0\Rightarrow x=10dxdS​=2x−2(20−x)=4x−40=0⇒x=10.  d2Sdx2=4>0\ \dfrac{d^2S}{dx^2}=4>0 dx2d2S​=4>0: minimum.

Parts: 101010 and 101010 (minimum sum of squares 200200200).

Similarly (Ex. 2.4 Q10): divide 303030 into two parts with maximum product: P=x(30−x)P=x(30-x)P=x(30−x), P′=30−2x=0⇒x=15P'=30-2x=0\Rightarrow x=15P′=30−2x=0⇒x=15, P′′=−2<0P''=-2<0P′′=−2<0; parts 15,1515,1515,15.

Wire bent into a rectangle [PYQ Jun 2026 Q22, 3 marks; Ex. 2.4 Q12; textbook Ex. 2 with 120 cm]

A wire of length 363636 cm is bent into a rectangle. Find its dimensions for maximum area.

Let length =x=x=x, breadth =y=y=y. Perimeter: 2(x+y)=36⇒y=18−x2(x+y)=36\Rightarrow y=18-x2(x+y)=36⇒y=18−x.

A=xy=x(18−x)=18x−x2A=xy=x(18-x)=18x-x^2A=xy=x(18−x)=18x−x2.  dAdx=18−2x=0⇒x=9\ \dfrac{dA}{dx}=18-2x=0\Rightarrow x=9 dxdA​=18−2x=0⇒x=9.  d2Adx2=−2<0\ \dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=-2<0 dx2d2A​=−2<0: maximum.

y=18−9=9y=18-9=9y=18−9=9. The area is maximum when the rectangle is a square of side 999 cm (area 818181 cm²).

Open box with square base [PYQ Mar 2024 Q32, 4 marks]

A box with a square base and open top has surface area 147147147 cm². Find its dimensions for maximum volume.

Let the side of the base be xxx cm and height hhh cm.

Constraint (base + 4 sides, no top): x2+4xh=147⇒h=147−x24xx^2+4xh=147\Rightarrow h=\dfrac{147-x^2}{4x}x2+4xh=147⇒h=4x147−x2​.

Objective: V=x2h=x2⋅147−x24x=147x−x34V=x^2h=x^2\cdot\dfrac{147-x^2}{4x}=\dfrac{147x-x^3}{4}V=x2h=x2⋅4x147−x2​=4147x−x3​.

dVdx=147−3x24=0⇒x2=49⇒x=7\dfrac{dV}{dx}=\dfrac{147-3x^2}{4}=0\Rightarrow x^2=49\Rightarrow x=7dxdV​=4147−3x2​=0⇒x2=49⇒x=7 (reject x=−7x=-7x=−7).

d2Vdx2=−6x4=−3x2\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{6x}{4}=-\dfrac{3x}{2}dx2d2V​=−46x​=−23x​; at x=7x=7x=7 it is −212<0-\dfrac{21}{2}<0−221​<0: maximum.

h=147−4928=9828=3.5h=\dfrac{147-49}{28}=\dfrac{98}{28}=3.5h=28147−49​=2898​=3.5.

Dimensions: base 777 cm ×\times× 777 cm, height 3.53.53.5 cm. (Maximum volume =49×3.5=171.5=49\times3.5=171.5=49×3.5=171.5 cm³.)

Ex. 2.4 Q17 is the same with 192192192 cm²: x=8x=8x=8, h=4h=4h=4. Notice h=x2h=\tfrac x2h=2x​ in both — for an open square-based box of maximum volume, height is always half the base side. That is a good check of your arithmetic.

Box from a square sheet by cutting corners (textbook Ex. 4)

Squares of side xxx are cut from the corners of an 181818 cm square card and the sides turned up.

V=(18−2x)2x=4x3−72x2+324xV=(18-2x)^2x=4x^3-72x^2+324xV=(18−2x)2x=4x3−72x2+324x.  V′=12x2−144x+324=12(x−3)(x−9)=0⇒x=3\ V'=12x^2-144x+324=12(x-3)(x-9)=0\Rightarrow x=3 V′=12x2−144x+324=12(x−3)(x−9)=0⇒x=3 or 999.

x=9x=9x=9 is rejected: the base side 18−2(9)=018-2(9)=018−2(9)=0.  V′′=24x−144\ V''=24x-144 V′′=24x−144, V′′(3)=−72<0V''(3)=-72<0V′′(3)=−72<0: maximum.

Maximum volume =(12)2(3)=432=(12)^2(3)=432=(12)2(3)=432 cm³.

Printed area on a sheet (textbook Ex. 3)

Sheet area 242424 m²; margins 757575 cm top and bottom, 505050 cm each side. Let width xxx, length yyy; xy=24xy=24xy=24.

Printed area A=(x−1)(y−1.5)=(x−1)(24x−1.5)=25.5−1.5x−24xA=(x-1)(y-1.5)=(x-1)\left(\dfrac{24}{x}-1.5\right)=25.5-1.5x-\dfrac{24}{x}A=(x−1)(y−1.5)=(x−1)(x24​−1.5)=25.5−1.5x−x24​.

A′=−1.5+24x2=0⇒x2=16⇒x=4A'=-1.5+\dfrac{24}{x^2}=0\Rightarrow x^2=16\Rightarrow x=4A′=−1.5+x224​=0⇒x2=16⇒x=4; A′′=−48x3<0A''=-\dfrac{48}{x^3}<0A′′=−x348​<0: maximum. y=6y=6y=6.

Paper: width 444 m, length 666 m.

Textbook misprint

The textbook writes “−1.5x+24x2=0-1.5x+\tfrac{24}{x^2}=0−1.5x+x224​=0” for A′=0A'=0A′=0; the stray xxx is a typo. It should be −1.5+24x2=0-1.5+\tfrac{24}{x^2}=0−1.5+x224​=0, which is what leads to x=4x=4x=4.

Triangle with two given sides (textbook Ex. 5)

Δ=12bcsin⁡A\Delta=\tfrac12bc\sin AΔ=21​bcsinA.  dΔdA=12bccos⁡A=0⇒A=π2\ \dfrac{d\Delta}{dA}=\tfrac12bc\cos A=0\Rightarrow A=\dfrac\pi2 dAdΔ​=21​bccosA=0⇒A=2π​;  d2ΔdA2=−12bcsin⁡A<0\ \dfrac{d^2\Delta}{dA^2}=-\tfrac12bc\sin A<0 dA2d2Δ​=−21​bcsinA<0. Maximum area when the angle between the given sides is π2\dfrac\pi22π​.

Cone of given slant height (textbook Ex. 6)

Slant lll; height xxx, radius rrr: r2=l2−x2r^2=l^2-x^2r2=l2−x2.  V=13πr2x=π3(l2x−x3)\ V=\tfrac13\pi r^2x=\tfrac\pi3(l^2x-x^3) V=31​πr2x=3π​(l2x−x3).

V′=π3(l2−3x2)=0⇒x=l3V'=\tfrac\pi3(l^2-3x^2)=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{l}{\sqrt3}V′=3π​(l2−3x2)=0⇒x=3​l​; V′′=−2πx<0V''=-2\pi x<0V′′=−2πx<0: maximum. Then r=l2−l23=2 l3r=\sqrt{l^2-\tfrac{l^2}3}=\dfrac{\sqrt2\,l}{\sqrt3}r=l2−3l2​​=3​2​l​.

Semi-vertical angle α\alphaα: tan⁡α=rx=2⇒α=tan⁡−12\tan\alpha=\dfrac rx=\sqrt2\Rightarrow\alpha=\tan^{-1}\sqrt2tanα=xr​=2​⇒α=tan−12​.

Covered box, base x×3xx\times3xx×3x, fixed volume — minimum surface (textbook Ex. 7)

V=3x2hV=3x^2hV=3x2h (constant), S=2(3x2)+2(3xh)+2(xh)=6x2+8xhS=2(3x^2)+2(3xh)+2(xh)=6x^2+8xhS=2(3x2)+2(3xh)+2(xh)=6x2+8xh.

Since VVV is constant, dVdx=0\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0dxdV​=0: 3x2dhdx+6xh=0⇒dhdx=−2hx3x^2\dfrac{dh}{dx}+6xh=0\Rightarrow\dfrac{dh}{dx}=-\dfrac{2h}{x}3x2dxdh​+6xh=0⇒dxdh​=−x2h​.

dSdx=12x+8(xdhdx+h)=12x+8(−2h+h)=12x−8h=0⇒h=3x2\dfrac{dS}{dx}=12x+8\left(x\dfrac{dh}{dx}+h\right)=12x+8(-2h+h)=12x-8h=0\Rightarrow h=\dfrac{3x}{2}dxdS​=12x+8(xdxdh​+h)=12x+8(−2h+h)=12x−8h=0⇒h=23x​.

d2Sdx2=12−8dhdx=12+16hx>0\dfrac{d^2S}{dx^2}=12-8\dfrac{dh}{dx}=12+\dfrac{16h}{x}>0dx2d2S​=12−8dxdh​=12+x16h​>0: minimum. Height =32×=\tfrac32\times=23​× shorter side of base.

This example teaches a technique: when the constraint is awkward to solve, differentiate it implicitly instead.

How 4-mark optimisation answers are usually marked (typical scheme, not an official one)

Your project folder has the question papers but no official marking schemes, so this split is the usual pattern rather than a verified one: about 1 mark for forming the objective in one variable, 1 mark for differentiating and solving f′=0f'=0f′=0, 1 mark for the second-derivative test, 1 mark for the final dimensions/value. Skipping the second-derivative test is the most common way to drop a mark.
